Lessons.Title: Non-unit Fractions on the Number Line
ExplanationParagraphs: 2021 warm-up Choral Count: One-fourths begins at 1/4, writes four fractions on each row, makes four rows and STOPs at 16/4. Each next term increases the numerator by 1 while the denominator remains 4. Row endings 4/4, 8/4, 12/4 and 16/4 correspond to 1, 2, 3 and 4 wholes. Teacher asks learners to explain patterns, not just list numbers.

This source lesson explicitly INTRODUCES the vocabulary NUMERATOR (how many equal unit-fraction pieces) and DENOMINATOR (how many equal parts partition ONE whole). The preceding first-edition lesson on non-unit shaded fractions delayed these technical names, so their introduction HERE is sequence-specific.

Activity 1, Number Line Scoot Stage 2: students work in pairs with an original multi-number-line gameboard, a number cube, each student's recording sheet and ten or more base-ten cubes used as pieces. Place a marker at zero on each available number line; roll the number cube, record and move the matching count of fractional INTERVALS on a selected line. Objective: land on the FINAL TICK MARK labeled 4 with as many markers as possible. From 3/4, a move of four 1/4 intervals reaches 7/4, not 4; do not confuse rolling 4 intervals with automatically reaching line-end 4. The precise publisher-specific blackline Stage 2 Gameboard and Stage 2 Directions were referenced, but their original pixels/text were not licensed, embedded or fully verified here. Teacher checks rule compliance and the actual recorded moves.

Activity 2, Fractions on the Number Line, has exactly four original pairs: 3/4 and 6/4; 7/8 and 12/8; 2/3 and 4/3; 2/6 and 7/6. On each 0-to-2 blank number line, make equally spaced 1/denominator intervals; count the numerator steps from zero. Respect both fractions in every pair, including those >1: 6/4=1+2/4, 12/8=1+4/8, 4/3=1+1/3, 7/6=1+1/6.

In original Activity 2 reflection, ask how to make eighths and locate 7/8 and 12/8 on the same unit-length scale, and what patterns emerge as numerators pass denominators. Do not reduce 7/8 and 12/8 to two unrelated generic topics. The point at 12/8 lies at 1 and 4 eighths on the SAME 0-to-2 line.

Activity 3, What's the Fraction?, is a pupil-created, OPEN task: partition an unlabeled 0-to-2 number line into any equal-size intervals, mark but DO NOT WRITE the selected fraction, trade lines with a partner, determine the partition and marked fraction, defend reasoning, and optionally repeat. There is no single fixed fraction or a deterministic source answer to this partner's invented drawing. Teacher reviews both marked lines and interpretation.

Lesson synthesis visually counts one-fourth steps to 3/4 (1/4,2/4,3/4), emphasizing a fraction as a NUMBER AT THE END of the measured length. Original Cool-down is gated and titled Where is 5/3?; only the heading is public, not the publisher assessment prompt. Original publisher gameboard is not reproduced, and Stage D/tests have not been executed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Numerator and denominator vocabulary
KeyConcepts.Definition: Denominator names how many equal fractional parts form a whole; numerator counts how many such parts.
KeyConcepts.Rule: n/b counts n successive unit intervals of length 1/b, including across whole-unit boundaries.
KeyConcepts.Example: 7/6 is seven sixth-length jumps, ending one sixth beyond 1.

KeyConcepts.Title: More than one whole
KeyConcepts.Definition: A non-unit fraction a/b can be greater than 1 when a>b.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Locate b/b at 1, then count a−b more 1/b intervals.

KeyConcepts.Title: Choral sequence
KeyConcepts.Definition: Adding one 1/4 each step increases only the top number by one.
KeyConcepts.Rule: k/4 then (k+1)/4, for k=1 through 16 in the source warm-up.

KeyConcepts.Title: Open game evidence
KeyConcepts.Definition: Actual outcome depends on game moves, shared gameboard and pupils' choices.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Record every chosen fraction interval and verify whether the marker lands exactly on final mark 4.
KeyConcepts.Example: A roll of 4 on a quarters line moves four 1/4 spaces, or distance 1.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original 3/4 and 6/4
WorkedExamples.Question: On the same number line, locate 3/4 and 6/4.
WorkedExamples.Method: Partition 0-to-1 into denominator equal spaces and count numerator spaces.
Steps: Set endpoints zero, one and two.
WorkedExamples.Check: The first is below 1; the second is above 1.

WorkedExamples.Title: Number Line Scoot — moving four quarters
WorkedExamples.Question: If the piece is at 3/4 and the roll means four quarter intervals, where does the piece end?
WorkedExamples.Method: Add interval lengths before comparing with target 4.
Steps: This is NOT the 4-endpoint of the gameboard.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original quarter count to 16/4
WorkedExamples.Question: Continue one-fourth counting, four terms per row.
WorkedExamples.Method: Keep denominator 4, add 1 to numerator each time.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: 2021 source explicitly continues through 16/4 across four rows.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep counting unit fourths across four wholes.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat 6/4, 12/8, 4/3 or 7/6 as impossible to plot.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original 0–2 source lines include values beyond 1.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Complete one full set denominator/denominator, then count remaining intervals into the next whole.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume a four-interval move from 3/4 automatically reaches whole-number 4.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The move distance is 4/4=1; resulting coordinate is 7/4.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Distinguish the numbered die count, fraction step size and absolute endpoint.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Give a unique answer to What's the Fraction? created by pupils.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The pupils choose their own equal partition and marked location.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Have partner read and defend the particular marked line; teacher checks actual work.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use numerator and denominator formal labels as if introduced in the preceding unit5 lesson3.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original teacher narrative formally introduces these terms in this 2021 lesson.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Introduce them during today's choral-count synthesis.

SummaryPoints: One-fourth Choral Count: exactly 16 terms, four rows, from 1/4 through 16/4.
Numerator and denominator vocabulary introduced in THIS lesson's warm-up synthesis.
Number Line Scoot Stage2 uses two players, separate recorded fractional jumps and multiple zero-to-four lines; no fixed play transcript.
Four original fraction pairs on 0-to-2 lines: 3/4 & 6/4; 7/8 & 12/8; 2/3 & 4/3; 2/6 & 7/6.
What's the Fraction? is an unlabelled student-created mark and reciprocal partner analysis, teacher-reviewed.
Original gameboard blacklines, gated assessment, student PDF and Stage D/test execution are not certified.
